maskingFinding: The reason all fifteen survive on macOS: resolvePointer:308 reads `onDiskSpelling(abs) ?? spellingViaRealpath(p, baseAbs, abs)`, and on macOS `realpathSync.native` DOES canonicalise case (measured: realpathSync.native('<dir>/SRC/Guard.TS') returns '<dir>/src/guard.ts', while plain realpathSync echoes the typed case). So for a plainly written pointer the realpath fallback re-derives the same verdict and hides anything the segment walk gets wrong. That is why `pointer-grammar.test.js`'s `file:SRC/Guard.TS` case and the whole net stay green with the case rung cut. Two pointer shapes escape the mask and were used to isolate the walk: (a) a pointer carrying a redundant `./` segment, because spellingViaRealpath compares the pointer STRING against the canonical suffix and `./x` never matches it; (b) a pointer that leaves the three bases but stays inside the enclosing repository, which takes resolvePointer:316 where `onDiskSpelling(abs)` is called with NO fallback behind it.

verdicts.evidence: Ran scripts/mutation-probe.mjs (corrected, --strict) on all seven missions plus the self-gate: identical `check --strict --json` payload every time (8/8 'no observable difference'). Ran the whole net (unit suite, smoke, OSCAL, in-toto, audit corpus, self-gate --strict) with the sibling mutant at the same line applied: all six legs exit 0. COULD NOT CLEAR. This mutant forces `cur = sep` unconditionally, which is a no-op only while `parts[0] === ""` — true for every path this function receives on POSIX, and measured rather than read: onDiskSpelling is only ever called with a `path.resolve()` result, and `path.posix.resolve` yields an empty component at index 0 and nowhere else ('/a/b'.split('/') -> ['','a','b']; resolve('//x/y','z').split('/') -> ['','x','y','z'], the '//' collapsed). On win32 the same measurement gives win32.resolve('C:\\proj','src\\a.ts').split('\\') -> ['C:','proj','src','a.ts'], so the mutant would set cur to '\\' instead of 'C:\\' — a drive-RELATIVE walk, which is verbatim the defect the first windows-latest CI leg found on 2026-08-17 and which this line exists to fix. I have no Windows runner here and the suite has no win32 fixture, so nothing in runward's net can distinguish this mutant on any platform. Filed as a hole per the rule that an undecidable mutant is over-reported, not cleared. The work it names is shared with the four mutants below: make the drive-root computation reachable by a test (extract it as an exported pure function taking a path flavour, or add a win32-only fixture that plants a mis-spelled pointer).

verdicts.argument: The mutated expression is the condition of `parts[0] === "" ? 1 : 1`. BOTH arms are the same literal `1`, so the value of the condition cannot reach the loop variable: `i` is initialised to 1 whatever the condition evaluates to. The condition is a pure string comparison with no side effect, so evaluating it or not is also unobservable. This holds for every input and every platform — it is a property of the expression, not of the data — so no mission can distinguish it. (Worth noting to the author, though not a defect: the ternary is vestigial and reads as if it once branched 1/0; a reader will assume it decides something.)

verdicts.evidence: Identical `check --strict --json` payload on all seven probe missions and the self-gate (8/8).
verdicts.argument: Same expression, opposite constant. `parts[0] === "" ? 1 : 1` yields 1 for a true condition and 1 for a false one, so forcing the condition to `false` selects the other arm of a ternary whose two arms are the identical literal. `i` is 1 either way; the discarded comparison is pure. No input on any platform can make the two programs differ.

verdicts.evidence: Identical `check --strict --json` payload on all seven probe missions and the self-gate (8/8).
verdicts.argument: Negating the comparison swaps which arm of `? 1 : 1` is taken. Both arms are the literal `1`, so `i` is initialised to 1 in both programs for every value of parts[0]. The comparison itself is pure. Nothing downstream reads the condition. No mission, on any platform, can distinguish them.

verdicts.evidence: Identical `check --strict --json` payload on all seven probe missions and the self-gate (8/8).
verdicts.argument: Changing the right-hand operand only changes which arm of `? 1 : 1` is selected — and both arms are the literal `1`. `parts[0] === "Stryker was here!"` is a pure comparison whose result is discarded by construction. `i` is 1 in both programs for every input, on every platform. This is a mutant of a value that no longer feeds a decision, so no mission can distinguish it.

verdicts.evidence: Identical `check --strict --json` payload on all seven probe missions and the self-gate (8/8), including the four missions where the walk alone decides and M3 where any extra or missing verdict would show as a false red or a false green.
verdicts.argument: The mutant runs the loop body once more, with `i === parts.length`. `parts` is an Array, so `parts[parts.length]` is `undefined`; `want` is therefore `undefined`, and the FIRST statement of the body is `if (!want) continue`, which is taken because `!undefined` is true. `want` is not read before that guard, and the guard's branch touches neither `cur` nor `differs` nor `entries`. Control then reaches `i++`, making `i === parts.length + 1`, which fails `i <= parts.length`, so the loop terminates. The extra iteration is therefore a no-op with respect to every value the function returns, for any input and on any platform (the reasoning uses only array indexing past the end and the falsiness of `undefined`). Note the coupling, stated so a later reader does not mistake it: this equivalence holds because the `!want` guard is present in the unmutated program.

verdicts.evidence: Identical `check --strict --json` payload on all seven probe missions and the self-gate (8/8 'no observable difference'). COULD NOT CLEAR. Removing the `!want` skip only matters when a path component is empty. Measured, not read: onDiskSpelling only ever receives a `path.resolve()` result, `path.posix.resolve` collapses '//' (resolve('//x/y','z').split('/') -> ['','x','y','z']) and produces an empty component at index 0 only, while the loop starts at index 1 — so on this platform the guard never fires and no mission can reach it. The one shape that does reach it is a Windows UNC or extended-length path: win32.resolve('\\\\server\\share','x\\y').split('\\') -> ['','','server','share','x','y'] and '\\\\?\\C:\\proj' -> ['','','?','C:',...], both with an empty component at index 1. I cannot run either here, and the suite has no win32 fixture, so nothing in runward's net distinguishes this mutant on any platform. Filed as a hole rather than argued equivalent, per the rule that an undecidable mutant is over-reported. It shares the remedy of the five drive-root mutants above: one exported, path-flavour-parameterised walk that a unit test can feed win32-shaped input to.

summary.note: The 6 unclearable ones are one region, not six findings: the drive-root/segment bookkeeping at lines 257 and 261, which is unreachable from any mission on a POSIX machine (measured) and which the suite covers on no platform. One remedy closes all six — expose the root computation and the segment walk as a path-flavour-parameterised pure function a unit test can feed win32-shaped input to, or add a windows-latest leg that plants a mis-spelled pointer. The 4 directly observed ones are two distinct pieces of work: a case-divergent pointer in a shape spellingViaRealpath does not answer (three mutants), and a pointer under an unlistable directory (one mutant).
